evaluation.positioning_hook: A broke Brooklyn painter is recruited to forge a lost masterpiece for a trans art-world insider, only to get trapped between class resentment, family money, and an FBI sting.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible and commercially sticky: art-world intrigue, class tension, and a con with a built-in sting. It’s still a sharper specialty buy than a broad four-quadrant play, because the pleasure depends on art-market specificity and character dynamics.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast and cleanly in the opening stretch: Ross needs money, Brett needs leverage, and the forged painting becomes the engine. The script keeps the central proposition clear even as it deepens the scheme with provenance, authentication, and the FBI.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ross is a vivid underdog with real contradiction—technically gifted, socially self-sabotaging, and emotionally legible. Brett is equally strong as a high-status operator with wounded need underneath the swagger, and their friction gives the movie its charge.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script finds a fresh lane by making the forgery story about labor, authorship, and who gets to be seen, not just about crime mechanics. The art-world process details and the class satire give it a confident, ownable angle.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The scheme escalates in clean stages—recruitment, research, fabrication, authentication, sting, aftermath—and the reversals keep it moving. The middle does lean on explanation and art-world discourse at times, which slows the propulsion relative to the strongest con-thriller versions of this lane.

resonant_originality.reasoning: It feels fresh because the forgery isn’t just a plot device; it becomes a story about value creation, class access, and the politics of recognition. The ending’s pivot to Ross’s own work and the Boys & Girls Club workshop makes the premise feel earned rather than merely clever.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The New York art ecosystem is rendered with unusually specific texture: Christie’s restoration, galleries, collectors, consultants, freeports, provenance games, and the social codes around all of it. The world generates story at every turn and feels lived-in rather than researched.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is distinctive: satirical, intimate, and intellectually playful without losing emotional stakes. The script can move from art-market jargon to bedbug eviction to a Narcan rescue and still feel like one coherent register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the con plot is a deeper argument about meritocracy, authorship, and who gets to claim genius. Ross’s father, Brett’s family wound, and the final classroom reveal all suggest a movie with more emotional afterlife than the premise initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ross/Brett/Amara is a strong triangle, and each pairing produces different energy: mentorship, manipulation, rivalry, attraction, and betrayal. Even supporting figures like Mullet Queer, Stephen, and the Billionaire have enough texture to keep the social world active.

lead_characters.name: Ross Tom
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s, Brooklyn-based painter; working-class/financially precarious; white.
lead_characters.hook: Ross is a technically gifted oil painter with a self-defeating streak and a humiliatingly precarious life: eviction notice, student debt, dead-end art-world access, and a talent that keeps getting praised in the wrong language. She’s funny when cornered, painfully sincere when she shouldn’t be, and most compelling when she’s trying to turn private feeling into visible form.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Greta Gerwig in Frances Ha or Abbi Jacobson in Broad City when the role is built around awkward intelligence, self-awareness, and emotional exposure. It gives an actor the chance to play comic embarrassment, class resentment, and real artistic conviction in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Brett Banneker
lead_characters.demographics: Trans woman, 20s, wealthy New York art-world operator; Yale-educated; family-money adjacent.
lead_characters.hook: Brett is a polished, hyper-competent social climber who talks like she’s already won, but the script keeps revealing how much of that armor is built from family damage and a desperate need to be taken seriously. She’s funny, ruthless, wounded, and genuinely moved by art, which makes her both dangerous and magnetic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Ayo Edebiri in The Bear when the role lets an actor weaponize wit while letting hurt leak through the seams. It also has the prestige-antihero electricity of Jodie Comer in Killing Eve, but with more emotional specificity and social satire.

lead_characters.name: Amara Chaudhry
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s, South Asian; elite art consultant with Yale pedigree and strong social fluency.
lead_characters.hook: Amara is the script’s most openly transactional operator: charming, predatory, and always one step ahead until the consequences catch up. She’s not just a villain; she’s the embodiment of the art world’s extraction machine, which makes her useful, funny, and deeply dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the razor-sharp social menace of Sarah Snook in Succession or Aubrey Plaza in Ingrid Goes West. The fun is in playing someone who can smile through a theft and still sound like the smartest person in the room.

lead_characters.name: The Billionaire
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s-60s, ultra-wealthy collector and father; white; tech-money elite.
lead_characters.hook: He’s a volatile patriarch whose taste, ego, and grievance all point in the same direction. The script uses him as both a family wound and a market force, which makes him less a cartoon rich guy than a pressure system with a pulse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do controlled menace with flashes of hurt, like Jeremy Strong in Succession or Michael Stuhlbarg in The Trial of the Chicago 7 when the power dynamic is the performance. It’s a deliciously specific rich-man part with real scene-stealing potential.

lead_characters.name: Stephen Forster
lead_characters.demographics: Man, late 20s-30s, lawyer; polished, upper-class, queer-coded or socially fluid in presentation.
lead_characters.hook: Stephen is the quiet utility player who turns out to be more useful than anyone expects, especially when the story needs legal finesse and a clean exit. He’s not flashy, but the script gives him a dry intelligence that makes him feel like a real person inside the machine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the sly competence of Matthew Macfadyen in Succession or Ben Schwartz in a prestige-comedy lane when the joke is that he’s the smartest calm person in the room. It’s a strong supporting part with a late-game payoff.

lead_characters.name: Mullet Queer
lead_characters.hook: Mullet Queer functions as Ross’s emotional barometer inside the artist ecosystem: someone who knows the hustle, knows the compromises, and still wants to believe in the work. The character adds community texture and gives the movie a lived-in art-scene voice.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do scene-stealing specificity the way Patti Harrison or Bowen Yang can in a sharp ensemble. It’s a compact but memorable part with real cultural texture.

casting_characteristics: Lead requires a painterly, intelligent, emotionally exposed performer in her 20s
Brett requires a trans woman performer with high-status ease and sharp comic timing
Several supporting roles are age-flexible but depend on credible art-world fluency

technical.vfx_details: Mostly invisible or compositional work for paintings, signage, and a few stylized inserts; no major digital spectacle.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical painting/fabrication process, Narcan overdose beat, auction-room crowd control, and some controlled security/FBI action.

rights_flags.detail: Brock Colyar / Brock Collyer is a named real-world media figure reference.
Christie’s, the Met, the Whitney, Yale, and the Boys & Girls Club of New York are depicted as real organizations.
Daily Mail, Uniqlo, Wendy’s, TikTok/phone apps, Narcan, and other named consumer brands appear on the page.
The script references The Sheltering Sky, Law & Order, and art-history materials such as catalogue raisonné and lecture content that may require clearance review depending on usage.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: specialty theatrical with strong streaming afterlife, or prestige streamer original with awards positioning.

budget.note: Contemporary New York plus a Portugal travel block, multiple museum/gallery interiors, and a few auction-house crowd scenes keep this above a contained indie, but it stays well away from effects-heavy scope.

casting.note: The lead needs a very specific mix of painterly credibility, comic self-embarrassment, and emotional openness, while Brett needs a trans performer who can play elite social command without flattening the vulnerability underneath.

development.note: The script is clear and commercially legible, but the art-world jargon, the con mechanics, and the final legal/ethical pivot around forgery versus homage will need careful buyer-facing framing.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like smart, character-driven prestige thrillers with art-world satire, class tension, and morally messy women at the center.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, skewing female but with strong appeal to art-world, indie-film, and prestige-drama audiences across genders.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary New York locations, a short Portugal travel block, and a mostly practical art-world production design footprint keep this in the specialty indie lane.

lane_fit.lane: A24-adjacent prestige indie with crime-thriller DNA
types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams building adult female-led prestige lanes
producer-director packages looking for awards-friendly character material
mid-budget genre buyers with taste for social satire
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where smart, adult, high-concept character pieces can play theatrically and then travel on streaming. The art-world specificity gives it a premium sheen, while the con structure keeps it commercially readable.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The story resolves the Ross/Brett/Amara triangle cleanly, and no side character is built as a clear franchise anchor.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The art-world is story-generating, not decorative.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the movie a premium, specific world buyers can market without needing a giant budget. It will attract executives and directors who want a prestige setting that naturally produces conflict, status games, and visual texture.
strengths.evidence: Christie’s restoration grotto, freeports, provenance lectures, gallery openings, and the authentication process all drive plot.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ross is a rare lead role for an actor.
strengths.what_it_means: The part can launch or reframe a performer because it combines comic humiliation, class pain, and genuine artistic authority. That makes it attractive to casting directors looking for a breakout showcase rather than a generic heroine.
strengths.evidence: Her disastrous grant interview, the failed sales pitch at the Armory, and the bedbug/eviction spiral all sit beside her real painterly talent.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Brett gives the movie its voltage.
strengths.what_it_means: She turns the story from a simple forgery caper into a volatile relationship drama with real emotional and social stakes. Buyers respond to that because it creates a second star part and a dynamic that can carry the whole movie.
strengths.evidence: Her gallery ambition, family wound, and eventual betrayal of Ross all reveal a character who is both strategist and wounded child.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The premise has a clean commercial engine.
strengths.what_it_means: A forgery scheme with an FBI sting is easy to pitch and easy to track, which helps the movie travel in the marketplace. It gives the project a hook that can sell on premise alone while still rewarding character-driven execution.
strengths.evidence: The plan to paint, authenticate, and then expose the fake drives the entire back half of the script.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending converts the con into a thesis.
strengths.what_it_means: That makes the movie feel smarter than a standard crime caper and gives it awards-friendly thematic lift. It also broadens the audience beyond genre buyers to viewers who want a statement about labor, value, and authorship.
strengths.evidence: The final gallery reveal, the Boys & Girls Club workshop, and Ross’s line that talent is everywhere but opportunity isn’t.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The movie is built for strong word of mouth.
strengths.what_it_means: It has a lot of quotable, socially legible material—art-world snobbery, class humiliation, and betrayal—that audiences will repeat after seeing it. That helps specialty theatrical and streaming discovery alike.
strengths.evidence: The consultant commission talk, the “ghost painting” idea, and the final public reveal all have memorable, talkable beats.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, marketable prestige indie: a female-led art-world con movie with a clean hook, a breakout lead role, and a world that feels expensive without being expensive to make. The script pairs a commercially legible forgery engine with real emotional stakes and a final thematic payoff, which gives buyers both a pitch and a reason to care.

items.area: The middle leans hard on explanation.
items.detail: The provenance, authentication, and art-history material is rich, but several stretches function as lecture as much as drama. That’s not a deal-breaker, but it does mean the movie’s momentum depends on the audience enjoying the specificity rather than just following the scheme.

items.area: Ross’s passivity is a real buy-side question.
items.detail: For long stretches she is being recruited, corrected, and maneuvered by Brett and Amara before she fully asserts herself. Buyers will notice that the lead’s agency is strongest in the back half, which makes the early act a little more conditional than the premise suggests.

items.area: The art-world specificity narrows the audience.
items.detail: The movie is strongest when it is deep in the weeds of collectors, consultants, freeports, and authentication culture, but that same specificity makes it a specialty play rather than a broad commercial title. That’s fine, but it should be positioned as a prestige lane buy, not a mass-market thriller.

items.area: Brett’s betrayal lands late but needs trust.
items.detail: The emotional turn works, but it asks the audience to invest in a relationship that is partly transactional for most of the runtime. That makes the final reveal potent, but also means the movie is carrying a meaningful trust burden in the third act.

items.area: The legal logic is carefully threaded.
items.detail: The script smartly avoids a clean forgery sale, but the distinction between homage, fake, and attempted fraud is doing a lot of work. That’s a strength on the page, yet it also means the buyer conversation will likely include questions about how cleanly the legal stakes read to a general audience.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is that its smartest material is also its most explanatory: the art-world mechanics are vivid, but they slow the engine whenever the movie pauses to teach. The other buyer-side question is Ross’s early agency; once the con is in motion the movie snaps into place, but the first act is more dependent on the audience buying the world than the lead driving it.
